## The surprising education of Christopher Nolan
For someone who loves film so much, it might be surprising to learn that Christopher Nolan did _not_ go to[ film school.](https://studyinternational.com/news/best-film-schools/)
But he studied something maybe just as relevant, if not _more._ He pursued English Literature at University College London (UCL).
It wasn’t that Nolan didn’t try pursuing film. Years after graduating, [Nolan was interviewed](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/0/what-was-like-teach-christopher-nolan-director-ucl/) by a film professor, Professor Philip Horne. Nolan told him, “Your film class is the only film class I’ve done in my life. It was bloody irritating, actually. No fault of yours. In a good way, it put me off ever studying film in that way, because if you want to be a filmmaker, I couldn’t sit there; it’s much easier to do it with books. With films, I was already too conscious of the compromises you make every day on set.”
With literature, he got to pick up a whole new way of thinking about storytelling: he’s talked about how novelists have had narrative freedom for centuries (flashbacks, unreliable narrators, jumping around in time) that filmmakers had gotten boxed out of once TV made linear storytelling the default.
That idea — steal the freedom novelists always had — basically became his whole directorial thesis. Memento’s reverse chronology, Inception’s nested dream layers, Tenet’s inverted time, Dunkirk’s three overlapping timelines — all of it can be traced back to his literary background.
While he was studying at UCL, though, something that was highly relevant for him was the Union Film Society, where he became president and started shooting 16mm films. He also funded his summer film projects by screening movies during term time.
It was scrappy, self-taught, guerrilla-style filmmaking — the same DIY instincts he used to make his first feature, Following (1998), on a budget of roughly US$6,000, reportedly.

## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Slade_School_of_Fine_Art&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/SLADE_1905_B_sampled.jpeg/250px-SLADE_1905_B_sampled.jpeg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:SLADE_1905_B_sampled.jpeg)Students at the Slade in 1905
The school was founded in University College on 2 October 1871 following an endowment from the will of the lawyer and philanthropist [Felix Slade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felix_Slade "Felix Slade") (1788–1868) who bequeathed £35,000 to establish three Chairs in [Fine Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_Art "Fine Art"), to be based at Oxford University, Cambridge University and [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London"). An additional six scholarships of £50 per annum were endowed to University College. The college itself provided £5000 to build the Slade School as part of the college quadrangle in Gower Street, premises which the School still occupies today.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slade_School_of_Fine_Art#cite_note-5)
Distinguished past teachers include [Henry Tonks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Tonks "Henry Tonks"), [Wilson Steer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Steer "Wilson Steer"), [Randolph Schwabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Schwabe "Randolph Schwabe"), [William Coldstream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Coldstream "William Coldstream"), [Andrew Forge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Forge "Andrew Forge"), [Lucian Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucian_Freud "Lucian Freud"), [John Hilliard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hilliard_\(artist\) "John Hilliard \(artist\)"), [Bruce McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_McLean "Bruce McLean"), [Alfred Gerrard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Gerrard "Alfred Gerrard") and [Phyllida Barlow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phyllida_Barlow "Phyllida Barlow").
